---
title: "Graphs as Matrices — Count Paths With Multiplication"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

Three rooms are joined by one-way doors. How can a computer count routes consisting of exactly two doors?

## Understand the central idea

An adjacency matrix records which direct edges exist. Squaring it counts length-two walks through possible intermediate vertices.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
(A^2)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{ik}A_{kj}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** A is an adjacency matrix with entries A_ij equal to 1 when a directed edge i→j exists and 0 otherwise; A² is its matrix square; i,j name start and destination nodes; k is an intermediate node; Σ adds possible intermediate routes.

**Substitute real numbers:** Let rooms 1→2, 2→3 and 1→3 be the only doors. A=[[0,1,1],[0,0,1],[0,0,0]]. Entry (A²)₁₃ is A₁₁A₁₃+A₁₂A₂₃+A₁₃A₃₃ =0+1+0=1. Exactly one two-door route connects 1 to 3, via room 2.

## Why this works

A length-two walk must select an intermediate vertex k. The product A_ik A_kj is 1 exactly when both required doors exist, so summing these products counts valid walks.

## What can go wrong?

For graphs with parallel edges, weights or probabilities, matrix multiplication has different interpretations. A walk may revisit vertices; it is not always a simple path.

## Your turn

Add a door 3→1. How many two-step walks begin and end at room 1?
